pool.prompt: A state DOT permit agency requires a submittal of your proposed route plan for a road-crossing permit. Which file format is most appropriate?
choices: KMZ — it opens in Google Earth and any field tablet
Shapefile — the standard GIS exchange format with full attribute data
PDF/A — the ISO archival PDF standard required for long-term records and formal permit submissions
DWG — the AutoCAD native format, since the DOT has engineers
pool.explanation: Permit agencies that archive records for years require PDF/A because it is self-contained — all fonts embedded, no external references, guaranteed identical rendering at any future date. KMZ requires Google Earth; a shapefile is a data format, not a printable plan; DWG requires AutoCAD and is the working format, not a submission format.

pool.prompt: You are delivering a shapefile of proposed pole locations to the design engineer. Which files must be included in the zip archive for the shapefile to be usable?
choices: Only the .shp file — the others are optional extras
The .shp (geometry) and .dbf (attributes) files only
The .shp, .shx, .dbf, and .prj files — all four are required
The .shp and a .kmz file for visual reference
pool.explanation: A shapefile is a family of files: .shp (geometry), .shx (spatial index, required for fast access), .dbf (attribute table), and .prj (coordinate reference system definition). Missing the .prj means the shapefile will import without a known coordinate system and may land in the wrong location.

pool.prompt: What is the practice of labeling each revision of a deliverable file with a date and revision number, so all recipients know which version they're working from, called?
choices: Archiving
Versioning
Metadata tagging
Provenance logging
pool.explanation: Versioning prevents the common and costly mistake of an engineer or field crew working from a superseded survey file. A proper version label includes both the revision number and the date, e.g. 'RouteA_SurveyPackage_v2_2026-05-01.zip.'

pool.prompt: A field crew member needs to check proposed pole locations on their smartphone while walking the route. Which format is most appropriate?
choices: Shapefile — it contains the most complete attribute data
KMZ — it opens in Google Earth on any smartphone with no GIS software required
GeoTIFF — it provides the highest-resolution imagery
PDF/A — it renders identically on any device
pool.explanation: KMZ is the field-crew-friendly format — free Google Earth app on any smartphone, tap a location to see notes. Shapefile requires GIS software; GeoTIFF is a raster image format without clickable attributes; PDF/A is a static printable document without interactive GPS-synchronized positioning.

pool.prompt: Why does a single OSP route survey project typically require delivering the SAME underlying data in multiple formats (KMZ, shapefile, PDF/A) rather than just one universal format?
choices: Multiple formats are required purely by regulatory mandate with no practical purpose

Different recipients need different capabilities: field crews need a lightweight app-friendly viewer (KMZ), the design engineer needs full attribute/GIS data (shapefile), and permit agencies need an archival, self-contained document (PDF/A) — no single format serves all three needs well
Format choice makes no practical difference; any one format would work equally well for all recipients
Multiple formats exist only because GIS software cannot standardize on one format
pool.explanation: Each format serves a distinct audience and use case: KMZ for lightweight mobile field access, shapefile for GIS-software-based engineering work with full attribute data, and PDF/A for long-term archival permit submissions — the differing needs justify producing multiple format deliverables from the same underlying survey data.

pool.prompt: A recipient opens a delivered file named 'FINAL_FINAL_USE_THIS_ONE.kmz.' What problem does this naming convention illustrate?
choices: No problem — the name clearly communicates this is the correct file to use

It is the opposite of proper versioning — there's no way to tell how many revisions preceded this file or when it was created, risking someone unknowingly working from an even-more-superseded copy later
KMZ files cannot be renamed under any circumstances
This naming convention is required by RUS for all final deliverables
pool.explanation: Ad hoc labels like 'FINAL_FINAL' provide no structured information about revision sequence or creation date, defeating the purpose of versioning — a future recipient has no reliable way to confirm this is truly the most current version.

pool.prompt: Why might a design engineer specifically request the shapefile format rather than the KMZ, even though KMZ is easier to open?
choices: KMZ files cannot contain any location data at all

The shapefile preserves the full attribute table (pole numbers, heights, notes, and other tabular fields) in a format GIS software can directly query and analyze, while KMZ's simpler structure is optimized for visual display rather than data-rich engineering analysis
Shapefiles are always smaller in file size than KMZ
KMZ files expire after 30 days and become unusable
pool.explanation: Shapefiles integrate directly into GIS analysis workflows with their full attribute data intact, which is what a design engineer needs for engineering work — KMZ prioritizes easy visual access (e.g., on Google Earth) over GIS-analysis-ready data structure.

pool.prompt: What is the risk of submitting a route plan permit application as a DWG file to a state DOT permit reviewer who may not have AutoCAD?
choices: No risk — DWG is a universal format readable by any software

The reviewer may be unable to open or properly review the submittal at all, since DWG is a proprietary AutoCAD-native working format, not a universally accessible or long-term-archival document format like PDF/A
DWG files automatically convert themselves to PDF when opened by non-AutoCAD software
DWG is required by all state DOTs and no alternative format would be accepted anyway
pool.explanation: DWG is the design engineer's native working format, requiring AutoCAD (or compatible CAD software) to open — not a safe assumption for every permit reviewer. PDF/A is the appropriate submission format precisely because it's self-contained and universally viewable without specialized software.
